California’s Proposition 43 Adds a New Chapter to State’s History of Local Tax Limits
Aravind Boddupalli
Display Date
October 27, 2026
Next month, California voters will decide whether to require a two-thirds vote for voter-initiated local special taxes, or taxes dedicated to a specific purpose.
Proposition 43 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/43/index.htm) would reverse a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) that have allowed these measures to pass with a simple majority, raising their approval threshold to the same one that local lawmakers face to enact these taxes. If passed, it would apply to measures placed on ballots on or after January 1, 2027.
While cities, counties, and special districts provide essential services, including fire protection, roads, parks, and libraries, their ability to raise taxes is governed by a complicated set of statewide rules. Proposition 43 could further constrain local governments’ ability to raise revenue, even for services supported by a majority of voters.
California’s fiscal history and comparisons with other states offer some perspective on what the change could mean for local governments and the communities they serve.
California's fiscal rules are nearly 50 years in the making
Proposition 43 joins a lineage of statewide measures (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/2669) that reshaped local public finances starting in the late 1970s. A few notable examples:
Proposition 13 (1978) capped property tax rates and required two-thirds voter approval for local special taxes, which later came to be defined as taxes dedicated to special purposes.
Proposition 218 (1996) added restrictions on local governments' ability to raise revenue, including new simple majority voter-approval requirements for new general taxes and property-related fees.
Proposition 39 (2000) lowered the voter threshold for qualifying school facility bonds from two-thirds to 55 percent, moving in the opposite direction.
Proposition 26 (2010) broadened the definition of taxes subject to voter approval.
The result is a complicated set of institutional rules where revenue changes face different voter-approval requirements depending on their type, how revenue will be used, and whether voters or legislators placed the proposal on the ballot.
California is not the only state revisiting supermajority requirements in November. Voters in South Dakota and Utah (https://www.multistate.us/elections/ballot-measure?id=21126) will consider measures that would require higher approval thresholds for certain tax or constitutional changes. But California's debate is different: It centers on voter-initiated local tax measures rather than statewide tax initiatives or statewide constitutional amendments.
The California Budget and Policy Center (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-california-voters-approve-proposition-43/) identifies several recent voter-initiated special taxes that passed with a simple majority vote. Examples include San Francisco’s tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, and Fresno’s increase of its local sales tax rate to fund community parks.
What the revenue patterns reveal
According to TPC’s analysis of the 2024 Census Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances (https://state-local-finance-data.taxpolicycenter.org/pages.cfm), California ranked 37 th among states on the share of local general revenue coming from own-source revenues, like taxes, fees, or charges, rather than federal or state government transfers (Figure 1).
Since 1977, just before Proposition 13 began reshaping California's local finances, growth in local own-source revenue has trailed growth in state own-source revenue, although some of this reflects different tax bases at each government level, including the state's reliance on income taxes and local governments' heavier reliance on property taxes and fees (Figure 2).
Together, these figures suggest that California's local governments remain somewhat reliant on state decisions and intergovernmental funding streams. However, local governments continue to deliver many public services. This disconnect can weaken efficiency and accountability, as noted (https://lao.ca.gov/analysis_1993/MGMS_reprint_02-93.html) by the state's Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO).
And, if Proposition 43 makes it more challenging for local governments to raise revenues, local lawmakers may need to increase general taxes, reduce government spending, or look to state lawmakers to help foot their bills. Unlike special taxes, general taxes are not earmarked to be spent for a particular purpose. Voters who support a tax that specifically pays for child care or community parks may be less willing to support a general tax that goes into a government's general fund and could be spent across a wide range of activities.
Further, localities within California differ substantially in wealth, economic opportunity, and fiscal capacity. Jurisdictions with stronger property tax bases and local economies can often generate more revenue from the same available tax policy than communities with fewer resources (https://www.gfoa.org/materials/addressing-resource-inequities). If dedicated local revenues from special taxes are harder to secure, those disparities in fiscal capacity and maintenance of services between poorer and wealthy jurisdictions could widen, raising potential equity (https://taxpolicycenter.org/publications/state-and-local-government-revenues-and-racial-disparities) concerns (https://taxpolicycenter.org/publications/more-than-fines-and-fees-incorporating-equity-city-revenue-strategies).
California has seen before how voting rules affect tax measures
Prior research (https://www.ppic.org/publication/fiscal-effects-of-voter-approval-requirements-on-local-governments/) found that voter approval rates vary considerably by type of revenue measure, with transportation, fire protection, and education-related measures receiving the most support.
And after Proposition 39 lowered the approval threshold for school facility bond measures in 2000, passage rates increased by nearly 30 percent, according to the LAO (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Detail/2978), even though average share of voters supporting the measures remained roughly flat.
California’s voting rules create a contradiction
Voters often prefer taxes dedicated to a specific purpose (https://www.californiacityfinance.com/ReformVoteSwap.pdf), yet California generally requires higher approval thresholds for those taxes than for general taxes.
Proposition 43 would extend the two-thirds approval requirement, which currently applies to local lawmakers, to voters who propose local special taxes. Supporters could argue that requiring broader agreement protects taxpayers from increases that lack widespread support. But the higher threshold would also make it harder to pass tax measures that a majority of voters do support.
California’s history suggests that voter-approval thresholds matter. The question facing voters in November is whether requiring broader support for local special taxes is worth potentially limiting communities’ ability to raise revenue for public services.

Issue Brief
Should California Voters Approve Proposition 43?
What the Supermajority Vote Requirement for Local Special Tax Initiatives Would Mean for California Communities
August 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Issue Brief
key takeaway
Proposition 43 on the November ballot would require that at least two-thirds of local voters approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax, starting on January 1, 2027. As communities across California are facing substantial challenges and uncertainties, this measure would make it harder for local voters to raise revenues to support local public services and give outsized power to a small share of voters. Approval of the measure would decrease the likelihood that local governments meet the needs of their residents and could increase hardship in some communities throughout the state.

What Would Proposition 43 Do?
This measure would require at least two-thirds of local voters to approve any local initiative that would create, extend, or increase a special tax. The measure would apply to initiatives placed on a local ballot on or after January 1, 2027.
This new supermajority vote requirement would apply to special tax voter initiatives raising revenue for many types of local governments, including cities, counties, special districts, and other local or regional government entity. 1 (javascript:void(0)) Under California’s Constitution (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%202.&article=XIII%20C), all taxes levied by special districts are considered “special taxes,” so Prop. 43’s two-thirds vote requirement would apply to any taxes placed on the ballot by voters to generate revenues for special districts as well as city and county taxes for dedicated purposes.
Glossary of Key Terms
General tax
Local voter initiative process
Parcel tax
Simple majority vote
Special tax
Supermajority vote
General tax
A tax that is levied by a city or county and that may be spent on any program or service. All non-property taxes that cities and counties may levy can be imposed as general taxes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) . A general tax may be approved by a simple majority of local voters, regardless of whether it is placed on the ballot by the local government entity or by a local voter initiative.
Local voter initiative process
Gives residents of a city or a county the power to propose changes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%2011.&article=II) to local ordinances. This process involves a number of steps, including drafting a ballot measure, circulating petitions, and gathering the required signatures.
Parcel tax
A tax on a parcel of property that is not based on the property value. This tax is generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square-foot or per-room basis. Parcel taxes can be levied by cities, counties, school districts, community college districts, and most special districts. Parcel taxes are always considered to be special taxes for the purpose of determining voter-approval requirements.
Simple majority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive support from at least half of voters plus one additional voter (50%+1) in order to be approved.
Special tax
Includes (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.pdf) 1) parcel taxes, 2) city or county taxes (excluding property taxes) dedicated to specific purposes, and 3) taxes (excluding property taxes) levied by special purpose districts — that is, special districts, K-12 school districts, and community college districts.
Supermajority vote
A requirement that a state or local ballot measure receive more than a simple majority vote, such as three-fifths or two-thirds, in order to be approved.
What Are the Current Vote Requirements for Local Revenue Increases in California?
California’s Constitution has a complex set of rules governing how local governments can raise taxes and other types of revenue. These rules were put in place by statewide ballot measures over the past several decades (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Major%20Milestones%20in%20the%20Development%20of%20Voter%E2%80%93Approval%20Requirements%20for%20Local%20Taxes), beginning with Prop. 13 in 1978 and followed by other measures creating additional restrictions on local revenue-raising capacity, including Prop. 62 (1986) and Prop. 218 (1996).
These rules apply to local measures to create new taxes as well as to increase or extend any existing tax.
Tax measures proposed by local governments — such as city councils or county boards of supervisors — must go on the ballot and be approved by voters. Current voter-approval thresholds differ depending on the type of tax that would be raised:
A general tax requires only a simple majority vote to pass, with the revenue available for any program or service.
A special tax requires a two-thirds vote to pass, and includes a tax dedicated to a specific purpose.
Special taxes proposed through the local voter initiative process are subject to different rules. In recent years, a series of court decisions (https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-appeal/2021/a157983.html) have clarified that the two-thirds vote requirement for special taxes in the state Constitution does not apply to special tax measures placed on the ballot by local voter initiative. Therefore, both general taxes and special taxes proposed by voters can be approved with a simple majority vote . 2 (javascript:void(0)) Several cases involving special tax voter initiatives that were approved with a simple majority vote were appealed to the California Supreme Court, but the Supreme Court denied review of the appellate court decisions, allowing these decisions to stand. A variety of special tax initiatives have been approved over the past several years with a simple majority vote, such as:
San Francisco’s Measure C in November 2018, creating a tax on commercial landlords to raise funds for child care and early education, which passed with 51% of the vote.
Fresno’s Measure P in November 2018, increasing the local sales tax rate to fund community parks, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Los Angeles’ Measure ULA in November 2022, creating a property transfer tax on sales of high-value property to raise funds for affordable housing development and homelessness service, which passed with 58% of the vote.
Madera County’s Measure T in November 2024, renewing a local sales tax rate to fund transportation projects, which passed with 52% of the vote.
Certain types of local taxes are always classified as special taxes for the purposes of voter approval requirements. This includes:
Taxes levied by special-purpose districts, including school districts, community college districts, and special districts.
Parcel taxes, which are taxes on parcels of property that are not based on the property value . These taxes are generally levied at a flat rate per parcel, but can also be levied on a per-square foot or per-room basis.
What Services Do Local Governments in California Provide?
Californians in every community across the state benefit from services provided by local governments. Local services help keep people safe and healthy by providing fire protection, law enforcement, public health services, hospitals and emergency services, road safety, and more. Local governments also provide educational and recreational spaces like public libraries, public parks, and playgrounds.
Californians experiencing economic insecurity, food security, or who don’t have access to private health insurance can access financial assistance, food assistance, and health care because counties are there to administer public health and economic security programs. Cities can support the development of affordable housing to ensure more of their residents can afford a safe place to live.
The services provided by California’s local governments vary according to the type of entity (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/who_does_what.pdf):
Counties administer health and human services programs such as Medi-Cal (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/medi-cal/) health coverage, CalFresh (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calfresh/) food assistance, and CalWORKs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/topic/calworks/) cash assistance for families. Counties also provide public health, behavioral health, and child welfare services. Additionally, counties are responsible (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/california-county-budget-process-guide/) for overseeing the local justice system and courts, administering elections, and providing municipal services like sewer systems and trash pick-up in unincorporated areas.
Cities provide a variety of municipal services such as fire protection, housing and urban planning, parks and recreation, libraries, street repair, water and sewer systems, and law enforcement — although some of these services may be provided by special districts in some areas.
Special districts provide specialized services such as fire protection, water, electricity, parks and recreation, transit, hospitals, and other health care services.
Regional entities such as Joint Powers Authorities and Councils of Government coordinate policy and service provision across regions spanning multiple cities or counties, such as regional transportation authorities.
How Do Local Governments Raise Revenue?
Local governments in California rely on a variety of revenue sources, including transfers from the state and federal governments, allocations of local property taxes, and various other taxes, service charges, assessments, and fees.
Most types of local governments receive some revenues from the local property tax, capped at 1% by Prop. 13 (1978). Property taxes are collected by counties and the revenues are allocated (https://propertytax.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2026/revenue/0/entity_type?vis=pieChart) to support city and county governments, school districts, community college districts, and special districts in accordance with formulas established in state law. Local governments and voters cannot increase property taxes beyond the 1% rate, except to finance infrastructure bonds. 3 (javascript:void(0)) Property tax increases to support school infrastructure bonds can generally be approved by 55% of local voters. All other property taxes for infrastructure bonds must be approved by two-thirds of voters.

Other common types of taxes supporting local services include sales taxes (known as transactions and use taxes at the local level), taxes on hotel stays (known as transient occupancy taxes), property transfer taxes, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
The revenues that make up local government budgets vary by the type of entity (https://lao.ca.gov/reports/2014/finance/local-taxes/voter-approval-032014.aspx#Voter_Approval_Requirements_For_Taxes:~:text=Local%20Governments%20Levy%20Many%20Types%20of%20Taxes), and the legal authority to raise taxes (https://www.ca-ilg.org/sites/main/files/file-attachments/resources__Revenues_and_Responsibilities.pdf) also differs by government type. Cities and counties have fairly broad authority to raise a variety of taxes — with voter approval — while special districts have more limited authority. These districts are largely limited to parcel taxes — a tax on parcels of land not based on their value — as a source of discretionary revenue, although some can levy district sales taxes and certain other types of taxes.
More than half of county-level revenues (https://counties.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/category?vis=pieChart) statewide come from the state and federal governments and local property taxes. Other types of taxes make up a small share of total county revenues — generally less than 3%. Common types of taxes levied by counties include sales taxes, property transfer taxes, taxes on hotel stays, and utility user taxes.
City-level revenues (https://cities.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_1?vis=pieChart) primarily come from service charges for municipal functions — such as electricity, water, and sewer services — and various taxes. These two categories generally each make up around one-third of total city revenues statewide. Local property tax revenues and sales taxes are the largest sources of tax revenues for cities, each representing about one-quarter of tax revenues. Other major tax revenue sources for cities include taxes on hotel stays, utility user taxes, and business license taxes.
Special district revenues (https://districts.bythenumbers.sco.ca.gov/#!/year/2024/revenue/0/subcategory_2?vis=pieChart) come largely from customer service charges for the service provided by the district, local property taxes, and certain other taxes and assessments, depending on the type of district. 4 (javascript:void(0)) The composition of special district revenues depends on the type of special district (https://sgf.senate.ca.gov/sites/sgf.senate.ca.gov/files/special_district_facts_2016.pdf). Enterprise districts provide services to customers for a charge and operate similar to businesses, being largely financed by user charges. Examples of enterprise districts include health care districts, airport districts, water districts, and other utility districts. Non-enterprise districts provide benefits to entire communities — such as fire protection and road repair services — and are primarily funded by property taxes and other types of taxes and assessments. As noted above, taxes levied by special districts are always considered special taxes so they require approval of two-thirds of voters in the district, unless they are placed on the ballot by voters.
How Would Proposition 43 Affect California Communities?
Proposition 43 Would Make It More Difficult for Communities to Generate Revenues to Meet Local Needs
California already imposes high barriers to raising local revenues by requiring all special taxes levied by local governments to be approved by two-thirds of voters instead of a simple majority, and by classifying certain types of taxes — parcel taxes and taxes levied by special districts and school districts — as special taxes subject to higher vote requirements. Extending the two-thirds vote requirement to voter-initiated special tax proposals, as Prop. 43 proposes, would decrease the likelihood that these measures would pass, even if a significant majority of local voters support the measure and the services that the new revenues would fund.
In contrast to the high bar for raising taxes, local governments do not need voter approval to reduce services — and cuts to services often result when localities face revenue shortfalls. Yet, communities also have the option of raising revenues to help close budget gaps. If Prop. 43 passes, counties and cities would still have the ability to raise general taxes with approval from a simple majority of voters to shore up local services. However, local voters’ ability to propose new special taxes to protect or strengthen key services would be limited as local voter initiatives would become much more challenging to pass. Additionally, voters in special districts would face a higher bar to increase revenues to preserve and expand services, regardless of whether the funds would be targeted to specific programs.
Proposition 43’s Constraints on Local Revenues Would Make Things Harder for Communities Already Struggling
Governments across the board have felt the impacts of inflation on the costs of providing public services, and the state’s aging population increasing the cost of providing some services such as health care. The impacts of the 2025 federal budget reconciliation law, (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/hr1-and-the-federal-budget-how-california-leaders-can-respond-to-trumps-cuts/) H.R. 1 — also known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — along with the effects of climate change, the labor market (https://immresearch.org/reports/ice-arrests-result-in-a-decline-in-employment-state-level-projections/) and broader economic impacts (https://www.bayareaeconomy.org/files/pdf/Economic%20Impact%20of%20Mass%20Deportation_June%202025.pdf) of arrests and deportations of immigrants, and other federal policy changes such as tariffs, are also creating challenges for localities.

Proposition 43
Raise vote threshold for special tax measures
This would make it harder to impose or increase local taxes by raising the threshold for local citizen-driven special tax ballot initiatives to pass from a simple majority to two-thirds. The two-thirds threshold already applies to taxes proposed by local governments but not by individuals. The measure reflects a deal between state lawmakers and the anti-tax Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to keep a more restrictive tax proposal off the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

On the California Secretary of State’s website describing qualified statewide measures for the November ballot, voters will see a three-word reference to Proposition 43 referring to “Local taxes: limitation.”
It’s ironic the initiative that has sparked the most backroom drama in years is depicted with such little fanfare.

If voters approve it, Prop.
43 would close a court created loophole that allowed some local special taxes to evade the two-thirds vote requirement — taxes for specific items such as transit, housing, flood control and parks.

By The Mercury News/East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/the-mercury-newseast-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 17, 2026 at 4:30 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 19, 2026 at 11:22 AM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
California voters have twice approved initiatives making it harder to raise local government taxes — only to have the courts erode them.
Proposition 43 would undo the latest judicial meddling by once again restoring a supermajority threshold for passage of special taxes. Voters should approve it.
There are primarily two types of local taxes:
• A general tax can be used for any legitimate government purpose and is often sought to bolster the budget of a cash-strapped agency.
• A special tax is restricted to a specific purpose such as the construction of a government building or the funding of public transit.
It’s the voting rules for the latter that are at issue with Proposition 43.
Whereas general taxes require a simple majority voter approval for passage, special taxes, under Proposition 13 in 1978 and Proposition 218 in 1996, required two-thirds — until 2017.
That’s when the state Supreme Court, in an unrelated case, distinguished between measures (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/19/californias-supreme-court-has-thrown-cities-and-citizens-into-chaos-over-local-taxes/) placed on the ballot through initiative signature-gathering drives and those created by local government agencies.
Building on that court-created distinction, subsequent state appellate court rulings created a two-track system for passage of special taxes: Initiative measures require simple majority approval while those created by government agencies require two-thirds approval.

As a result, initiative special tax measures that had received more than a majority support, but less than two-thirds that had been thought necessary, have passed, including one for Alameda County (https://www.mercurynews.com/2020/03/06/borenstein-fight-over-alameda-county-sales-tax-hike-just-starting/) and one in Oakland (https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/10/17/borenstein-california-needs-clarity-on-vote-requirement-for-taxes/).
This is not what voters intended in 1978 or 1996. The route to the ballot should not determine the vote threshold for passage. Proposition 43 would overturn the court rulings and restore the two-thirds requirement for passage of special taxes.
Perverse incentives
Since 2017, we’ve seen the perverse incentives the court rulings have created. Government agencies have started turning to interest groups to qualify special taxes for the ballot.
For example, Measure RTM (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/09/endorsement-no-on-measure-rtm-transit-tax-bart-manufactured-crisis-vta-doesnt-have-one/), the regional transit sales tax measure voters are currently considering, could have been placed on the ballot by the Metropolitan Transportation Commission. But the measure would have then needed two-thirds voter approval. Instead, transit labor unions and contractors helped fund (https://thevoicesf.org/the-insiders-selling-measure-rtm/) an initiative signature drive and the subsequent campaign for the measure.
Similarly, in Oakland, the city last year put out a budget projection specifying the amount of money needed to fix a structural budget deficit and labor unions (https://netfile.com/public/COAK/campaign/filingsByMeasure/214936600-Measure%20E:%20Oakland%20Public%20Safety,%20Cleanliness%20and%20Community%20Accountability%20Act%20of%202026) then qualified a property tax measure for the June ballot (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/05/12/endorsement-oakland-measure-e-deceitful-tax-plan-broken-promisesn-another-deceitful-oakland-tax-plan-vote-no-on-measure-e/) for roughly that amount. (Amazingly, it failed to even muster majority support as voters recognized the long string of new taxes in recent years (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/06/05/oakland-tax-measure-e-fails/) had not been used for their promised purposes.)
In each case, the only reason backers qualified the measure through the initiative process was to bypass the two-thirds requirement — to bypass the intent of Propositions 13 and 218.
Reform needed
That said, it is past time for California voters to rethink their approach to property and other local taxes.
First, there are the backwards incentives that stemmed from court interpretations of the language Proposition 13 added to the state Constitution: “Cities, Counties and special districts, by a two-thirds vote of the qualified electors of such district, may impose special taxes on such district … .” (emphasis added)
While backers intended “special taxes” to refer to any levies beyond the Proposition 13 limit of 1% of assessed value, the Supreme Court subsequently narrowed that to mean taxes for a specific purpose. That interpretation was cemented with the passage of Proposition 218.
Consequently, we now distinguish between special taxes for specific purposes that require two-thirds approval (unless qualified through an initiative signature-gathering drive) and general taxes, which require a majority vote and can be used for any legitimate government purpose.
It’s backwards: The tax measures with the fewest restrictions are the easiest to pass. That’s why we often see local governments claiming they want money for a specific purpose but placing measures on the ballot that allow any use of the money.
A glaring example this election season is Palo Alto’s Measure J (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/14/endorsement-reject-palo-alto-nov-3-measure-j-sales-tax/), placed on the ballot by the City Council there. The measure, a proposed sales tax increase that requires majority support, is purportedly to purchase and upgrade a community center. But the tax would be permanent, and a future council could use the sales tax money for any purpose.
Property tax unfairness
Second, there’s the fundamental unfairness in Proposition 13, which not only set rules for passage of local taxes but, more significantly, governs how we tax property in California. The measure limits how much the assessed value of a property used to calculate the base tax can increase annually. But it then allows for a resetting of the assessed value when a property is sold.
The result is that people in identical houses can pay vastly different property taxes depending on when they bought their homes. It’s effectively a generational transfer of burden to newer homeowners, making the cost of housing greater for recent, including first-time, buyers.
It’s time to redistribute that burden — not to add to the total collected but to apportion it fairly in a revenue-neutral way between all property owners.
Finally, the debate over the rules for passage of local taxes and for rethinking how we tax property should be carried out in a holistic fashion, not piecemeal. And it should be decided by voters, not by the courts.
In the meantime, Proposition 43 would merely restore the intent of voters who passed the two prior measures. It merits support.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: August 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: August 28, 2026 at 12:16 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
On the California Secretary of State’s website describing qualified statewide measures for the November ballot, voters will see a three-word reference to Proposition 43 referring to “Local taxes: limitation.” (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/qualified-ballot-measures) It’s ironic the initiative that has sparked the most backroom drama in years is depicted with such little fanfare.
Prop. 43 was placed on the ballot by a panicked California Legislature after a last- minute deal was struck with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association to pull the association’s more sweeping Local Taxpayer Protection Act from the ballot. Despite the complicated inside-the-Capitol machinations with lobbyists and lawmakers, the resulting measure is rather simple.
If voters approve it, Prop. 43 (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/aca-22.pdf) would close a court created loophole that allowed some local special taxes to evade the two-thirds vote requirement — taxes for specific items such as transit, housing, flood control and parks. Specifically, tax increases that are placed on the ballot by citizens via signature-gathering.
This change would restore the threshold to the design of 1978’s tax-limiting Proposition 13. Since then, a series of bone-headed court decisions (https://www.hjta.org/california-commentary/courts-widen-the-door-to-even-more-local-taxes-in-california/) determined that voters could approve citizen-driven special tax increases by a simple majority, while maintaining the two-thirds rule for special tax increases directly placed on the ballot by local governments. This loophole led to abuses, as unions served as the cat’s paw for local officials by gathering signatures to place tax increases on the ballot and pass them with less than a two-thirds vote.
So, the bottom line: Vote yes on Proposition 43, as it will impede local governments from getting around the two-thirds vote for special taxes to bail themselves out of endless budget debacles. As the economy has stumbled and local governments have burned through “free” COVID money from Washington, D.C., municipalities increasingly are turning to bonds and tax increases (https://caltax.org/2026/03/20/voters-to-decide-fate-of-80-local-tax-and-bond-measures-in-june/) .
Money is fungible. If voters approve “special” (https://flooddistrict.marincounty.gov/question/what-is-a-special-tax/) taxes, that leaves more money in the general fund to spend as usual. That typically means bigger paychecks and pensions for powerful public-employee unions. The two-thirds vote threshold is one of the few ways that California taxpayers can at least try to force their elected officials to live within their means.
That said, we’re disappointed that the final measure doesn’t include a ban and rollback of local transfer taxes. For instance, Los Angeles’ disastrous “mansion tax” (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2025-10-01/apartment-development-pipeline-dries-up-in-spite-of-demand-for-housing) not only imposes astronomical rates on Angelenos who sell pricey homes (currently a 4% tax on homes priced above $5.4 million and 5.5% on those priced above $10.9 million) — but applies to apartment and commercial properties. Predictably, that has quashed housing production in Los Angeles.

The original initiative by HJTA banned real estate transfer taxes above a minor documentary transfer fee. Proponents ultimately pulled that initiative from the ballot at the last minute after the Legislature passed the compromise (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) measure that deals only with the two-thirds vote issue. The Legislature also agreed to pull a separate ballot measure designed to make it harder to pass all future tax-limitation efforts, including this one. This deal to remove the transfer-tax portion of the initiative led to a split within the business coalition that had supported it.
Complicating matters further, the key Democratic lawmakers who placed the current measure on the ballot are calling for voters to reject it. They placed it there simply as a means to derail something that they viewed as far worse (https://sdvoice.info/on-your-november-ballot-proposition-43/) because it protected taxpayers even more from the predations of government and allied special interests. But voters needn’t get caught up in the back story, however interesting as insight into Sacramento’s sausage-making process.
As it stands, the final measure is praiseworthy, as it puts the brakes on local governments’ ability to collude with special interests to more easily raise your taxes. Vote yes on Prop. 43 to make it harder to raise taxes.

Proposition 43, sponsored by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, may seem pretty basic. It is a constitutional amendment that would restore the two-thirds vote (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/08/california-constitution-proposition-43-taxes/) requirement to enact all local “special taxes” intended to fund a specific, designated purpose, such as public safety or libraries.
But the ballot measure is more accurately seen as Howard Jarvis giving voters a chance to tell the California Supreme Court to take a hike — to stop sabotaging popular state laws that create obstacles to newer and higher taxes. Just as Republican-appointed U.S. Supreme Court justices tailor their legal rulings to meet broad conservative objectives, some of the state supremes’ most important rulings feel contrived to achieve the goals of the liberal Sacramento establishment.
An obvious example is the court’s contrary rulings on citizen initiatives, which have long since lost their noble patina of being a way for voters to use “direct democracy” to overcome special interests. Instead, as political scientists and journalists have documented for decades, such measures are routinely stage-managed (https://digitalcommons.lmu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=3172&context=llr) by powerful forces — unions, business organizations and, yes, elected officials.
Sometimes the state’s justices choose to ignore this history. Sometimes they emphasize it.
In a 2017 case involving a ballot measure related to cannabis dispensaries in the city of Upland, the court, on a 5-2 vote, drastically changed (https://calmatters.org/economy/2019/02/local-tax-chaos-california-supreme-court/) how the judicial system interpreted voter-approved state laws, especially Proposition 13 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_13,_Tax_Limitations_Initiative_(June_1978)) — the landmark 1978 legislation that kicked off a national taxpayer rights movement. The majority held that since the measure reached the ballot because of a citizen signature-gathering campaign — instead of the direct action of a local government body — simple majority support was necessary for enactment, not the two-thirds vote specified in Proposition 13.
Why? Because, per Justice Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar, courts must “liberally construe the public’s statewide and local initiative power.” Yet it was literally undisputed that the Upland measure reached the ballot not because of a backlash to City Hall machinations from residents but because of a well-funded effort by a cannabis trade group.
But in 2018, the state high court unanimously agreed (https://www.rstreet.org/commentary/public-sector-unions-win-big-at-the-california-supreme-court-in-getting-san-diego-pension-reforms-overturned/) that a 2012 ballot measure approved by a huge majority of San Diegans that ended defined benefit pensions for most new city hires should be invalidated (https://www.rstreet.org/commentary/public-sector-unions-win-big-at-the-california-supreme-court-in-getting-san-diego-pension-reforms-overturned/). Why? Because the fact that 116,000 city residents signed the petitions to put the measure on the ballot was tainted by the strong support of then-Mayor Jerry Sanders, who was depicted as trying to get around laws that require the city to collectively bargain changes in employment terms.
What he was trying to get around was the fact that the City Council majority, allied with unions, bitterly opposed pension changes despite compensation costs eating up a massive and growing chunk of city budgets. As former City Attorney Jan Goldsmith wrote (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2012/02/29/initiative-process-is-first-power-reserved-to-the-people/), “Never in the history of California has there ever been a requirement to negotiate with labor unions over terms of a citizens’ initiative placed on the ballot by voter signatures.”
These rulings can’t be squared. The state Supreme Court treats the citizen initiative process as a sacrosanct part of state government that must be “liberally construed” when it comes to allowing tax hikes on a simple majority vote. Summary
California’s record-setting late budget of 2008 has again called into question the wisdom
of requiring a two-thirds vote of the legislature—a supermajority—to pass a state budget,
especially in an era of intense partisanship. But other than hindering the process of passing a
budget each year, what are the policy consequences of requiring a supermajority? This paper
examines this question, as well as the possible consequences of other constraints on California
governance. We compare state and local revenues and spending in California with other states
that are not so similarly constrained.
We find that in fact, there is not much distinctive about California’s revenue and
spending patterns compared to other, less constrained states. Overall state and local spending
in California has increased as agencies and local jurisdictions have found various other means
—such as charges, fees, bonds, and sales taxes—to make up for property taxes lost after the
passage of Proposition 13 in 1978 and other subsequent voter-imposed limitations.
Notwithstanding the view of some conservatives that the supermajority requirement
will constrain taxes and spending, the reality is that limiting government spending through
a supermajority budget requirement is like squeezing a balloon in the hope of reducing the
overall volume of air. The volume of air in the balloon will not diminish, but squeezing it will
distort its shape, creating bulges in places of less pressure. Institutional constraints such as the
supermajority threshold have reshaped the form and mix of California’s revenues and expendi-
tures to some degree, but have not served the conservative goal of limiting total state and local
spending. Moreover, many of the fiscal patterns found in California are similar to those in other
states that have far fewer institutional constraints, some of them with none. This similarity
results from larger political forces at work, including a decline in trust in elected officials to
make sound fiscal decisions, changing tastes in public services, and an aversion to higher
general taxes.
As in the 1990s, the 2008 budget stalemate has led to calls for constitutional reform. In
addition to the question of the supermajority vote, any systematic review of the budget process
such as ours must consider related problems: the ease with which groups can change the
budget through the initiative process, revenue stability, and the political disconnect between
the public’s demand for services and its willingness to pay for them.

Introduction
In 1933, California voters adopted a proposition requiring a two-thirds vote of the
legislature—a supermajority—if spending grew by more than 5 percent. In 1962, the spending
limit was dropped but the supermajority requirement remained. The result in 2008 is that
California makes it harder for its legislature to pass a budget than all but a few other states.
Over the years, numerous commissions and reform groups have suggested institutional fixes
for California’s fiscal problems, in the hope that better budget processes will lead to better fiscal
decisions. Five organizations over the last 15 years—the California Constitutional Revision
Commission, the California Governance Consensus Project, the California Budget Project, the
California Business Roundtable and the League of Women Voters of California—have all
recommended that California abandon the two-thirds threshold for a simple majority
(Simmons, 2002).
At a purely procedural level, the most important advantage of doing so is to increase the
chances of passing budgets on time. Until 2008, tardy budgets caused some inconvenience and
damaged the legislature’s reputation, but the fiscal consequences were not serious enough to
galvanize any reform effort. But the prolonged 2008 budget battle has created a more serious
crisis and has made the simple majority idea much more appealing. Moreover, with California’s
political parties and elected officials becoming more polarized, a budget rule that assumes
mutual compromise and bargaining looks impractical. It also raises a fundamental question:
Is there any good policy reason to have a supermajority budget rule?
Proponents of supermajority vote thresholds believe that there is—that more is at stake
than just legislative efficiency. They argue that higher thresholds lead to less government
spending, simply because they make it harder for lawmakers and voting majorities to increase
taxes or expenditures.
A supermajority requires that unless the size of the legislative majority party equals or
exceeds the threshold, that party will need the support of some minority party members, even
if the majority controls both the legislative and executive branches. Because the California
Legislature has been controlled by Democrats since 1974, the need for Republican support
should result in lower overall spending because of concessions that would advance that
conservative goal. (Of course, if the reverse were true, the supermajority requirement could be
used to forestall a cut in spending that Republicans want. This is a useful reminder that when
political circumstances change, the same rules can lead to a different policy outcome.)
The notion that high procedural hurdles will lower spending levels is based on some fairly
strong assumptions regarding the state’s economy, its ability to exploit non-tax revenue bases,
the depth of party unity, and the ease of making fiscal decisions at the ballot box. It also fails
7
to anticipate potentially important unintended or unpredicted fiscal effects, especially if officials
and interest groups adapt creatively to the freshly imposed limits on traditional taxes and find
new resources.
We compare California’s institutional constraints with other states, and then examine
the general academic evidence about the importance of such formal restrictions. Next, to see if
these constraints have resulted in some distinctive patterns, we compare California’s history of
local and state taxing and spending with small samples of similarly restricted and unrestricted
states. Lastly, we will examine what our findings mean for California in terms of the value of
future institutional reforms.
Constraints on California’s Fiscal Policymaking
Beginning with Proposition 13 in 1978, Californians have passed numerous measures to
restrict the state’s fiscal activities. Despite many debates, conferences, and blue ribbon
commissions warning of the problems of serial adoption of such restrictions, most have not
been changed or removed. As a result, California’s elected officials are institutionally
constrained in their ability to make budgetary and fiscal decisions, more so in fact than any
other state. There is little sign of imminent change. Few elected officials are willing even to
broach the topic of amending—much less abolishing—Proposition 13. The Constitutional
Revision Commission’s attempt in the early 1990s to amend the two-thirds provision required
for a budgetary vote in the state legislature proved futile. Only Proposition 39 in 2000, a
measure that reduced the level of voter approval needed to pass local school district bonds,
from two-thirds to 55 percent, moved in a less constraining direction.
Constraint can take many forms, and Table 1 displays several. First, there are direct
fiscal constraints, such as supermajority voting requirements that raise the threshold for raising
taxes or enacting a budget, and other statutes and constitutional provisions that specifically
limit state spending or revenues. Another meaning of fiscal constraint is to deny elected
representatives their customary monopoly of control over the budget. Hence, direct-democracy
states, which allow voters to override and limit the budgetary decisions of elected officials, are
more constraining in this sense. Lastly, constraints can mean limitations on the legislative
capacity to review and scrutinize budgets. Although no evidence indicates that term limits lead
directly to lower levels of taxing and spending, they have altered the budget process by
weakening the legislature’s incentives and abilities to participate in budgetary review and
oversight (Cain and Kousser, 2004). California has all three types of constraints: higher
thresholds and direct limits, shared budgetary responsibility, and limited legislative capacity.
As Table 1 shows, California is one of only three states with a supermajority budget vote
requirement; six other states require a supermajority vote under specific conditions only, such
as failure to enact a budget on time. California is one of 27 states that have adopted a spending
or revenue limitation. It is one of only 16 states that have adopted a legislative supermajority
requirement for all tax increases. Seven of these states, including California, require a two-thirds
vote, five have a three-fifths threshold, and four need a vote of three-fourths of the legislature.
California has very strict term limits: six- and eight-year limits for the assembly and state senate
respectively, and a lifetime ban on returning to office when terms expire. It also possesses
comparatively friendly direct democracy processes at both the state and local levels; these
enable voters with only a simple majority to weigh in on fiscal matters, using a constitutional or
statutory initiative, and gives them the ability to overturn legislative actions by referendum.

A number of scholars have addressed the contentious question of whether fiscal con-
straints even matter. Several statistical studies seem to show that across states, the adoption of
supermajority requirements for increasing taxes does reduce the amount of state taxation (Bails
and Tieslau, 2000; Knight, 2000; Besley and Case, 2003). Brian Knight estimates that constraints
reduce taxes as a proportion of state revenue by 1.7 percent to 3.6 percent, or about 0.2 percent
of the average state GDP. Timothy Besley and Anne Case estimate that supermajority rules
reduced state taxes by as much as 8 percent between 1960 and 1997. So, across states and on
average, there is statistical evidence that supermajority rules reduce taxation levels.
The evidence is mixed on the effectiveness of other constraints. Limits on state spending
expenditures or revenue are common. Colorado and Oregon have both, 21 states have
expenditure limits only, and three have revenue limits only. The academic evidence on whether
they make a difference finds that these limits either have no effects (Rueben, 1996) or even
“perverse” effects suggesting the limits are actually associated with higher spending (Besley
and Case, 2003)1.
Although the number and breadth of fiscal constraints in California are impressive, their
effectiveness rests on both political and socio-economic assumptions that may not hold.
Supermajority rules for the budget and for tax increases will restrict spending and taxes only if
all of the following conditions are met:
1. The majority party is smaller than the supermajority threshold, or if not, has
serious splits within its ranks;
2. The minority or dissenting majority party faction has a more conservative fiscal
position;
3. The majority is not able to pick off members of the minority with district-based
benefits;
4. One party controls the executive and legislative branches.
The last condition is especially important in light of the fact that divided government
has been the norm in California for much of the period since 1978. Except for the last two years
of the Jerry Brown administration and the five recall-interrupted years of the Gray Davis
administration, California has had Republican governors who have been more fiscally
conservative than the Democratic majorities in the legislature. This has made supermajority
rules less important than they otherwise would have been.
1 Besley and Case attribute this to endogeneity of the decision to adopt limits: States with high spending may be
more likely to adopt them.
11
In the last 25 years, the first and second conditions have prevailed in California, as has
the third, with the exception of some early Davis administration budgets. The fourth condition
has not. The Democratic majorities in the legislature have not been supermajorities and the
Republican caucus has been distinctly more conservative than the Democrats, especially on fis-
cal matters. Party discipline among Republicans has been strong, limiting the Democrats’ ability
to pick off support from their ranks. But the governor has been Republican for all but the five
years between 1998 and 2003.
Considering all of these, the conditions for supermajority rules to have the greatest
effect were during the latter part of the Davis administration. At that time, Republican party
discipline was strictly enforced, the Democratic majority was not large enough to carry a
supermajority, and an economic slowdown brought an end to surplus budgets and thus, the
ability to pick off dissidents in the other party with district benefits. But in most other years,
divided government was as much responsible for the shape of the budget as any other factor.
There is no specific cross-state evidence that the imposition of term limits has directly
affected state and local spending. Republicans and conservatives supported the term limits
initiative, Proposition 140, to a greater degree than did liberals and Democrats, but the initiative
did not result in the wholesale transformation of the legislature that some expected. Nonethe-
less, in the budget process it has clearly weakened the legislature relative to the governor, and
has diminished the incentive of assemblymembers in particular to invest time in budget sub-
committee work and oversight (Cain and Kousser, 2004): Although term-limited legislators
could be less worried about the electoral consequences of their subcommittee votes, they would
not have the time necessary to devote to mastering budgetary matters.
The availability of direct democracy options is an important part of the tax and spending
mix. As noted above, initiative states are more likely to have supermajority tax requirements
and spending and revenue limitations. They are also more likely to have term limits. In
addition, since the passage of Proposition 218 in 1996, local authorities in California need
majority voter approval for any increase in taxes and for most new property-based revenues.
The effect of Proposition 13 and Proposition 218 was to increase dramatically voters’ involve-
ment in fiscal decision-making. Kim Rueben and Pedro Cerdan report that between 1986 and
2000, there were more than 2,500 local tax and bond measures. Two-thirds of these were for the
approval of taxes and fees, and one-third were for bond measures (Rueben and Cerdan, 2003).
There is some evidence, perhaps because of all the above factors, that direct democracy states
have lower levels of spending (Matsusaka, 1995).
In summary, California has a broader array of fiscal constraints than most other states.
Some academic studies have shown that supermajority rules and direct democracy lead to
lower tax and spending levels. On the other hand, given that California has had divided
government 21 out of the last 30 years, there is reason to question whether the supermajority
budget rules have had that much of a constraining effect. Other evidence shows that direct

Proposition 43 aims to tackle what supporters call a “loophole” in the rules for enacting local tax measures. The system, admittedly, is strange, but it works. We recommend Californians vote no on Prop. 43.
If a city council or a board of supervisors asks voters to approve a special tax dedicated to a specific purpose such as fire protection or parks, it needs two-thirds of the vote to pass. If, instead, residents put the exact same tax on the ballot by gathering signatures, it needs only a simple majority.
Normally, who is asking should not matter. How much people pay and where the money goes are the same. But it is not that simple. Elected officials face a higher bar, which discourages them from putting every spending wish on the ballot. Residents who organize, qualify a measure and persuade a majority of their voting neighbors to support it have an easier path to fund the things they care about.
Prop. 43 would amend the state constitution to require two-thirds approval for special taxes proposed by residents, the requirement that special taxes proposed by local governments now face. If voters approve it, that change would apply to measures passed after Jan. 1, 2027.
Local tax measures in Sonoma County demonstrate the harm that could follow when little more than one-third of voters can block what most of their neighbors want.
In March 2020, supervisors placed Measure G on the ballot. It asked for a half-cent sales tax for fire services. It received 64.8% support, falling about 2 percentage points short of what it needed to pass. Firefighters and other county residents then gathered nearly 29,000 signatures to place Measure H on the March 2024 ballot. It passed with 61.7% support. Fire agencies have received nearly $46 million, according to their first financial reports.
In November 2024, residents also put Measure I on the ballot. It established a quarter-cent sales tax for child care and children’s health. It passed with nearly 63% support and will raise about $30 million a year.
Neither of those 2024 measures came from elected officials. Residents did the work and put both on the ballot. Under Prop. 43, both would have failed.
This year, Napa County’s Measure B, a citizen-qualified half-cent sales tax for wildfire preparedness, watershed protection and open space, needs only a majority. If it were on the ballot next year and Prop. 43 had passed, it would need two-thirds.
Prop. 43’s supporters argue that they are merely trying to close a “court-created loophole.” The original two-thirds requirement came out of Proposition 13, passed in 1978. However, state courts have concluded that the requirement restrains only local governments because the California Constitution reserves initiative power to the people.
Local councils and boards of supervisors can put a tax measure on the ballot with a vote. One can make a case that the two-thirds requirement serves as a necessary check on that power.
But citizens who seek to put a tax increase or any other measure on the ballot already face significant hurdles, not least gathering thousands of signatures from registered voters. That is not a loophole. It is a system with a real check on each path.
Prop. 43 arrives on the ballot as a political bargain to stave off an even more onerous initiative. It would not cut anyone’s taxes. What it would do is give a minority of voters a veto over funding local services such as parks, fire protection and child care that most of their neighbors want. Ironically, Prop. 43 needs only a simple majority to pass.
Vote no on Prop. 43.

Confused about how to vote on Proposition 43? Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 7:54 AM
Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html) is billed as a taxpayer protection measure that would “save” Proposition 13.
In reality, it would make it much harder for citizen groups in California to pass tax increases to help pay for critical services such as fire and police protection, flood control, health care facilities and road maintenance. It would also make it harder to fund libraries, parks and affordable housing programs that local governments simply can’t afford.
Prop. 43 seeks to raise the threshold necessary to pass citizen tax initiatives from a simple majority to a supermajority of 66.7%, which would mean 33.3% of voters would be calling the shots.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 43 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article316990490.html)
This is why the combined editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee (https://www.sacbee.com/), Modesto Bee (https://www.modbee.com/), Merced Sun-Star, (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/) Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) oppose Prop. 43. We strongly urge a “no” vote.
Prop. 43 would give the minority too much power. It would make it much harder for citizens to take matters into their own hands when governments can’t — or won’t — finance special projects that serve the public interest.
The ability to pass special taxes is especially important now, when wildfires, droughts and extreme weather leave so many communities vulnerable. Rather than waiting for disaster to strike — or depending on Washington or Sacramento for financial help that may never come — local tax measures can provide revenue to prepare for emergencies, whether it means hiring more firefighters, upgrading equipment or clearing flood channels.
What supporters say
Anti-tax groups, such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association (https://www.hjta.org/saveprop13_about_initiative/) andReform California (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/campaigns/stop-the-tax-hikes), say Prop. 43 would merely close a legal loophole used too often by special-interest groups to fund pet projects on the backs of taxpayers.
They say that Proposition 13, which was passed by voters in 1978, specifies that cities, counties and special districts can impose taxes earmarked for specific purposes only with the approval of a supermajority of voters.
Yet language in Prop. 13 and in a follow-up measure, Prop. 218, is somewhat ambiguous. It does not specify that citizen tax initiatives require a supermajority to pass. In a series of court rulings, judges found that they do not.
We weren’t convinced by Prop. 43’s backers, and voters should be skeptical, too. Nor should they buy into the notion that plenty of money is available if public officials would only stop wasting it on misplaced priorities.
“We can go through any budget, and I will find the cost savings to eliminate the need for a tax increase on any ballot in the state of California this cycle,” Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, the head of Reform California, told us.
Never mind that federal and state budget cuts have taken a huge financial toll on local government. Sacramento County, for example, faced a $101 million budget shortfall this year. Atleast half the deficit (https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/cue-web/#/main?uri=https://cue.gcp.misitemgr.com/webservice/escenic/container/ac765bdc-7f13-11f1-a011-277da135f0d0&mimetype=x-ece/container&extra=%7B%22package%22:%22ece-auto-gen-845e918b-ec6d-4d33-a61b-298f753a3360%22%7D) was attributed to cuts in the federal budget.
Communities rely on special taxes for basic services
Local governments have made foolish and, in some cases, corrupt spending decisions, and they should be held accountable.
But Prop. 43 ignores the fact that many communities have no other way to finance needed services.
Take the tiny community of Crockett, population 3,000, located in Contra Costa County.
Volunteers with the Crockett Improvement Association assumed responsibility for landscaping and maintenance of public spaces — a job that included picking up litter, trimming bushes and maintaining streetlights. But when the work became too onerous for aging volunteers, the group gathered signatures to put a $50-a-year parcel tax (https://ballotpedia.org/Crockett_Community_Services_District,_California,_Measure_L,_Maintenance_and_Landscaping_Tax_Initiative_(November_2022)) on the ballot. It passed by 62.78%.
That’s impressive support, yet under Prop. 43, the measure would have failed. Then what? Allow trash and weeds and overgrown bushes to encroach on public spaces?
From a practical standpoint, special taxes are the only way some specific needs can be met, and requiring supermajority approval can create hardships — and even dangers — for communities large and small.
A more reasonable threshold — say 55%, which is the margin required to pass school facility bonds — would be a fair compromise to consider in the future.
For now, voters must decide whether to allow a small minority of voters to dictate whether tax measures should pass. We don’t believe they should.
